vignette: Samir stands at the edge of the rehearsal studio, watching dust motes drift through the high windows. The floorboards are polished maple, but his eyes keep tracing the hairline fractures in the seams, translating them into cracked concrete. He was twenty-six when the city he grew up in became a grid of checkpoints and sirens. He remembers the Tuesday the grid went down permanently—the silence that followed heavier than the explosions. He was walking his neighbor’s daughter to school when the overpass buckled. The air turned thick with limestone dust and copper. He doesn’t remember running. He only remembers the rebar pinning his ribs and the way his brother’s hand slipped from his. When he finally clawed his way out three days later, the city was gone, replaced by a landscape of shattered glass and waiting tents. The call to prayer that once timed his days was replaced by artillery. He left with his clothes and a brother who didn’t make it out. The years after the war became a slow unraveling. Samir crossed borders, rebuilt, and learned to live in a place where the sky rarely screams. But his body never received the memo. At forty-one, he is a dancer now, his profession a quiet rebellion against the fragility he once witnessed up close. He teaches contemporary movement to a small company, shaping spines and tracing arcs with his hands. Yet when the music swells too quickly, his breath catches. His shoulders hike up instinctively. He tells himself it’s just preparation, but his nerves are wired to scan exits, to track the heavy tread of boots in empty hallways, to count how many times someone claps their hands—a sound that still makes his jaw lock and his fingers curl. Tonight, after rehearsal, he sits on the edge of his bed, the duvet pulled to his waist. His wife, Lina, sleeps beside him, her breathing even and deep. He used to love the weight of her head on his shoulder. Now, when she shifts in her sleep, his pulse jumps to his throat. He counts her breaths until it settles. In the mornings, he wakes before his alarm, his body taut, already braced for an impact that never comes. He showers in cold water, trying to wash off the phantom grit that clings to his skin. He drinks his coffee standing at the kitchen counter, eyes fixed on the street, watching for delivery trucks that turn out to be nothing but neighbors going to work. He still dances, but the movement has changed. The leaps feel less like flight and more like desperate escapes. In rehearsal, he catches himself holding his breath during a sequence that mimics falling. His director notices the tension in his legs, the way his foot strikes the floor with too much force. Samir apologizes, blames a pulled muscle, and adjusts. He doesn’t tell anyone that the sound of a dropped weight triggers a memory of a doorway buckling inward, of voices cut short. He doesn’t mention how he has started avoiding crowded places, how the grocery store aisles feel like choke points, how he always chooses the corner seat at restaurants, back to the wall, eyes on the door. Lina asks him about the past, but he has learned to speak in fragments. She knows he flinches at sudden noises, knows he wakes with sweat on his collarbone, knows that some days he cannot leave the apartment without checking the locks four times. She holds his hand when the tremors come, but he has noticed how she hesitates before embracing him after long silences. Dance remains his anchor and his battlefield. When he finally allows himself to move without resistance, his body remembers what the war tried to erase: grace, extension, surrender. For a few measures, the music carries him forward, and the studio floor feels like solid ground. But when the track ends, the quiet rushes back in, and Samir stands still, waiting for the next cue, the next breath, the next moment to decide whether to step forward or brace himself.
